name: Caro-Kann Advance
summary: The Caro-Kann Advance (1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5) frees Black's bishop before ...e6, solving the bad-bishop problem.
intro: The Caro-Kann Advance Variation arises after 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5, when White seizes central space and locks the pawns, but Black immediately develops the light-squared bishop to f5 before shutting it in with ...e6. This is the key difference from the French Defense, where the same bishop remains buried behind its own pawn chain. The result is a strategically clear middlegame in which Black enjoys a healthy, active bishop outside the chain and clear plans of counterplay with ...c5 and ...e6.
line: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining feature of the Advance Caro-Kann is the fate of Black's light-squared bishop. By playing 3...Bf5 before ...e6, Black develops the piece to an active diagonal rather than entombing it, sidestepping the chronic bad-bishop problem that plagues the French. White, in return, gains a broad space advantage with the pawns on d4 and e5 and typically builds with Nf3, Be2 and O-O, aiming to make the extra space tell in the long run. Black's counterplay is thematic and reliable: undermine the head of White's chain with ...c5, complete development with ...e6, and press on the queenside while White tries to expand on the kingside.

Much of the theoretical battle revolves around the f5-bishop. White frequently launches the g4 thrust to harass it, gaining kingside space and time; Black must decide whether to retreat the bishop, exchange it, or drop it back to g6 and h7 where it eyes the sensitive light squares around White's king. Because the pawn structure is so committal, both sides operate with well-defined plans rather than tactical chaos, which is why the line has a reputation for being solid and strategically transparent.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The most important modern approach is the Short System, named for the plan of quiet development with 4.Nf3 e6 5.Be2, when White simply castles, plays c3 and Nbd2, and waits to exploit the space edge without committing to sharp pawn pushes. The alternative and more aggressive path is the g4 advance, the Advance-proper attacking scheme, where White plays an early g4 to kick the f5-bishop; after the bishop retreats to g6, White may follow with h4-h5 or Ne2 and Nf4, seeking to trap or exchange it and open lines on the kingside.

In every main line Black's counterplay flows from the same levers. After ...e6 Black almost always strikes with ...c5, challenging d4 and freeing the position; the knights usually go to e7 and d7 (or c6), and the queen and rooks mass against the c- and b-files. If White overextends with g4 and h4, Black can target the loosened light squares and the base of the chain, so White must balance the ambition of the kingside pawn storm against the structural risks it creates.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Advance Variation is one of the oldest ways of meeting the Caro-Kann, but for much of the twentieth century it was overshadowed by the classical 3.Nc3 and the Exchange lines, partly because 3...Bf5 was thought to give Black an easy game. Its modern popularity owes much to the quiet, positional Short System, which recast the Advance as a low-risk way for White to nurse a space advantage rather than force matters, and it remains a mainstream weapon at every level precisely because it offers White durable pressure while Black keeps the good bishop and clear, healthy counterplay.

Solid and strategically clear, with well-defined plans for both sides.
